screens.title: Composition and Design Patterns for Game Objects
screens.narratorSegment: In this lesson we'll explore why composition often outperforms deep inheritance when building game objects, and how a few common design patterns help keep game code modular and maintainable. You will learn how to model 'has-a' relationships so characters, props, and systems remain flexible; we'll also examine the Singleton pattern so you can manage truly global services safely. Finally, we'll introduce the Component Pattern as the foundational approach used in modern engines to assemble game objects from small, reusable behaviors. For example, a player can contain a weapon object and swap it at runtime rather than changing its type in an inheritance tree. That simple shift improves flexibility, reduces coupling, and makes runtime behavior easier to test. Over the next screens you'll see concrete C++ code that demonstrates composing a Player with a Weapon, a robust Singleton example for managers like audio or input, and a component-based GameObject built with smart pointers. As we go, watch for common mistakes: failing to manage component lifetime, overusing singletons, or letting a class become a God object. By the end you'll be able to pick the right tool—inheritance, composition, or a pattern—for the problem at hand. Consider: when would swapping components at runtime simplify your design?

screens.title: Learning Objectives
screens.narratorSegment: These learning objectives ground the lesson in practical skills you can apply immediately. First, you'll be able to distinguish inheritance from composition by identifying 'is-a' and 'has-a' relationships in your game designs. That distinction matters because choosing the wrong relationship can make code brittle or hard to extend. Second, you will implement composition in C++ by composing objects and delegating behavior, which lets you swap behaviors like weapons or scripts at runtime without changing core types. Third, you'll understand the Singleton pattern: how to create a single global instance for managers and when that choice introduces testing or coupling problems. Finally, you'll grasp the Component Pattern used by modern engines to assemble GameObjects from small behaviors. Each objective includes practice steps so you can verify the competency by building and running simple examples. These skills collectively reduce tight coupling, increase reuse, and make large game codebases easier to maintain and extend.

screens.title: Inheritance vs Composition
screens.narratorSegment: Let's define both relationships clearly. Inheritance models an 'is-a' relationship: a derived class extends a base class and can substitute for it. Use inheritance when you need polymorphism that represents a genuine subtype — for example, an Enemy that must be treated as an Actor in a rendering or update system. Composition models a 'has-a' relationship: an object contains other objects and delegates behavior to them. In games, composition shines because behaviors like rendering, physics, or weapons are orthogonal and change at runtime. A common misconception is to use inheritance for every form of reuse: that quickly creates deep hierarchies that are rigid and lead to the fragile base class problem. Composition avoids that by keeping components focused and replaceable. A concrete example: instead of making Player inherit from SwordUser, BowUser, and MagicUser, a Player can have a Weapon object and swap instances at runtime. The practical significance is maintainability: changes in one component don't ripple across unrelated subclasses. Try this mental check: if you want to replace a behavior without changing the object's identity, prefer composition. Inheritance vs Composition means use inheritance for true subtype polymorphism and composition to enable replaceable behaviors and runtime flexibility.. In practical terms, when 'is-a' is appropriate and when to prefer 'has-a' for game entities. A concrete example makes the pattern visible, and a brief contrast helps prevent a common misconception. This matters because learners need the underlying reasoning before they can apply the idea confidently or notice where it breaks down. The main takeaway is that the concept should be understood as a meaningful pattern, not just a label on the screen.

content.html:
Module 3 › Chapter 2.3 › Inheritance vs Composition
Is-a (Inheritance)
Use when objects are true subtypes
  • Polymorphism is primary reason to inherit.
  • Good for substitutable behaviors that share an interface.
  • Can create deep hierarchies that become brittle over time.
Common mistake

Using inheritance for code reuse alone, instead of for true subtype relationships, which leads to fragile base classes.

Has-a (Composition)
Build objects from replaceable parts
  • Model behaviors as member objects or components.
  • Swap implementations at runtime without changing object identity.
  • Leads to more modular and maintainable code in large projects.
Pro tip

If you find yourself creating many sibling subclasses that only differ by a single behavior, refactor toward composition.

screens.title: Composition in C++: Player and Weapon
screens.narratorSegment: Now we walk through a concrete C++ example that demonstrates composition clearly. The Weapon class encapsulates name and damage and exposes an Attack method. The Player contains a Weapon as a member variable and delegates attack behavior to that Weapon. This design allows changing the weapon by assignment or by swapping the underlying object, so the Player's code remains unchanged. A common nuance is how constructors initialize member objects: if you embed a Weapon object directly as a value member, you must initialize it in the Player constructor's initializer list. If you need polymorphic weapons, store pointers or smart pointers to a Weapon base and use virtual functions. Watch for ownership concerns: if you copy a Player object, value members will be copied unless you manage them explicitly. The code example in the lesson demonstrates creation, attack delegation, and ChangeWeapon. Use this pattern to keep character logic focused while letting weapons evolve independently. content.html:
Module 3 › Chapter 2.3 › Player & Weapon
Key idea

The Player contains a Weapon and delegates attack behavior to it. This lets you change the Weapon implementation without modifying Player logic.

Example outputs
  • Weapon creation and destruction messages help verify lifetime.
  • PerformAttack calls Weapon::Attack which prints damage and name.
  • ChangeWeapon replaces the composed Weapon and prints an equipped message.
Misconception

Embedding objects as values always simplifies ownership. In practice, you may need pointers or smart pointers for polymorphic components or to manage shared resources.

C++ (abridged)
#include <iostream>
#include <string>

class Weapon {
private:
  std::string name;
  int damage;
public:
  Weapon(const std::string& weaponName, int weaponDamage)
    : name(weaponName), damage(weaponDamage) {}

  int Attack() const {
    std::cout << name << " attacks for " << damage << " damage!" << std::endl;
    return damage;
  }

  std::string GetName() const { return name; }
};

class Player {
private:
  std::string name;
  int health;
  Weapon currentWeapon; // Player HAS-A Weapon

public:
  Player(const std::string& playerName, int initialHealth, const Weapon& startWeapon)
    : name(playerName), health(initialHealth), currentWeapon(startWeapon) {}

  void PerformAttack() {
    std::cout << name << " prepares to attack!" << std::endl;
    currentWeapon.Attack();
  }

  void ChangeWeapon(const Weapon& newWeapon) {
    currentWeapon = newWeapon;
    std::cout << name << " equipped " << currentWeapon.GetName() << std::endl;
  }
};
Note: Use smart pointers for polymorphic Weapon hierarchies.

screens.title: Singleton Pattern in Games
screens.narratorSegment: The Singleton Pattern ensures a class has only one instance and provides a global point of access. It's commonly used for managers such as audio, input, or resource loading in games. The typical implementation includes a private constructor, a static member that holds the instance, a static GetInstance method to create and return the instance, and deletion of copy constructor and assignment to prevent duplicates. This pattern simplifies access to a global service, but it introduces trade-offs: singletons can increase coupling across systems, make unit testing more difficult, and create hidden dependencies. A subtle practical concern is cleanup: when the program ends you should release any allocated resources to avoid leaks. Use singletons sparingly for truly global services, and prefer dependency injection or passing references where coupling and testability matter. As a rule of thumb, ask whether the object must be globally unique; if not, prefer other techniques. Singleton Pattern in Games means use singleton for unique global services, but be mindful of coupling and testing consequences.. In practical terms, a single global instance for managers and the trade-offs involved. A concrete example makes the pattern visible, and a brief contrast helps prevent a common misconception. This matters because learners need the underlying reasoning before they can apply the idea confidently or notice where it breaks down. The main takeaway is that the concept should be understood as a meaningful pattern, not just a label on the screen.

content.html:
Module 3 › Chapter 2.3 › Singleton Pattern
What it is
A creational pattern that restricts a class to a single instance and provides a global access point.
Characteristics
  • Private constructor to prevent direct instantiation.
  • Static method GetInstance() to create or return the single instance.
  • Copy constructor and assignment operator are deleted to avoid duplication.
Trade-offs
  • Pros: Simple global access for managers, avoids passing references everywhere.
  • Cons: Tight coupling, harder to unit test, can become a God object if overloaded with responsibilities.
  • Best practice: Limit responsibility and provide explicit shutdown to free resources.
Implementation hint
Prefer returning a reference and consider thread safety for multi-threaded contexts. For simple engines, a single-threaded lazy initialization is common.

screens.title: Singleton Example and Trade-offs
screens.narratorSegment: Let's examine an AudioManager implemented as a Singleton and why you must guard against overuse. A typical AudioManager has a private constructor, static instance pointer, and a GetInstance method that lazily creates the instance. That makes it simple to call PlaySound from anywhere. The concrete benefit is convenience: systems across your codebase can request audio without passing references through layers. However, if you add unrelated responsibilities—loading resources, mixing, state tracking—the class becomes a God object, which is hard to test and change. A frequent misconception is that Singletons are inherently anti-patterns; they are a tool with trade-offs. Use them for a truly single global resource, but keep that class focused. When writing tests, provide a way to inject a mock or to reset the singleton state between tests so testing remains feasible. Finally, ensure that you provide an explicit Shutdown that deletes the instance and frees native resources to avoid leaks when your engine exits. The main takeaway is that the concept should be understood as a meaningful pattern, not just a label on the screen.

content.html:
Module 3 › Chapter 2.3 › AudioManager Singleton
AudioManager (concept)
// Private constructor, static instance, deleted copy/assign
class AudioManager {
private:
  AudioManager() { /* init audio system */ }
  AudioManager(const AudioManager&) = delete;
  AudioManager& operator=(const AudioManager&) = delete;
  static AudioManager* instance;
public:
  static AudioManager* GetInstance() {
    if (instance == nullptr) instance = new AudioManager();
    return instance;
  }
  void PlaySound(const std::string& name) { /* play sound */ }
  static void Shutdown() { if (instance) { delete instance; instance = nullptr; } }
};
Keep the manager focused: avoid mixing unrelated responsibilities. Provide test hooks or allow swapping with a mock for unit tests.

screens.title: Component Pattern: Building Blocks for GameObjects
screens.narratorSegment: The Component Pattern treats a GameObject as a container that owns multiple small, focused components. Each component handles one responsibility: transform for position, render for drawing, physics for collision and movement, and script for game logic. This pattern enables you to add or remove behaviors at runtime by attaching or detaching components, which is particularly useful for dynamic gameplay where entities change roles or abilities. Unlike inheritance, components don't form a rigid tree; they are independent modules that the GameObject composes. Modern engines build on this idea with the Entity-Component-System architecture for performance and scale. A misconception is that components are just simple member objects; instead, design them with clear update contracts and ownership semantics. Think about lifetime: who creates a component, who destroys it, and how the GameObject's Update delegates to each component. This clarity prevents memory leaks and keeps behavior modular. Component Pattern: Building Blocks for GameObjects means assemble gameobjects from focused components to enable runtime flexibility and avoid brittle inheritance hierarchies.. In practical terms, why components replace deep inheritance in modern engines. A concrete example makes the pattern visible, and a brief contrast helps prevent a common misconception. This matters because learners need the underlying reasoning before they can apply the idea confidently or notice where it breaks down. The main takeaway is that the concept should be understood as a meaningful pattern, not just a label on the screen.

content.html:
Module 3 › Chapter 2.3 › Component Pattern
Pattern mechanics
  • GameObject is a lightweight container with an ID and a component list.
  • Components implement a common Update interface and focus on a single concern.
  • GameObject::Update delegates to each component; components are detachable at runtime.
Runtime benefits
  • Attach render and physics to make an object interactive; remove physics to make it static.
  • Compose behaviors without changing class hierarchies or recompiling large base classes.
Analogy
Think of a GameObject as a toolbox and components as tools. You assemble the tools you need for each job without creating a new toolbox type.

screens.title: Implementing Component and Concrete Components
screens.narratorSegment: We'll implement a Component base class with a pure virtual Update method and three concrete components: RenderComponent, PhysicsComponent, and ScriptComponent. Each concrete class provides its own Update behavior that prints a message to the console, which helps verify the update loop. Important design details: make the destructor virtual to ensure concrete components clean up correctly; include a name or identifier for debug prints; and prefer smart pointers when adding components to a GameObject to ensure safe ownership and automatic deletion. A common pitfall is leaving Update signatures inconsistent or not marking destructors virtual, which can lead to undefined behavior when deleting derived instances through base pointers. This example uses unique_ptr ownership in the consuming GameObject to remove manual delete calls and avoid memory leaks. Implementing components this way prepares you to extend behavior without changing the GameObject interface. Module 3 › Chapter 2.3 › Component Implementation
Key code (concept)
class Component {
protected:
  std::string name;
public:
  Component(const std::string& compName) : name(compName) {}
  virtual ~Component() { std::cout << "Component destroyed: " << name << std::endl; }

};

  std::string modelPath;
public:
  RenderComponent(const std::string& path) : Component("RenderComponent"), modelPath(path) {}
  void Update(float deltaTime) override { std::cout << "  " << name << ": Rendering model from: " << modelPath << std::endl; }
};

  float mass;
public:
  PhysicsComponent(float objMass) : Component("PhysicsComponent"), mass(objMass) {}
  void Update(float deltaTime) override { std::cout << "  " << name << ": Applying physics for mass: " << mass << std::endl; }
};

Key takeaway

Smart pointers express intent and avoid manual cleanup errors, especially in complex game object graphs.

C++ (GameObject excerpt)
#include <vector>
#include <memory>

class GameObject {
private:
  std::string id;
  std::vector<std::unique_ptr<Component>> components;
public:
  GameObject(const std::string& gameObjId) : id(gameObjId) {}
  ~GameObject() { std::cout << "GameObject destroyed: " << id << std::endl; }

  void AddComponent(Component* comp) {
    components.push_back(std::unique_ptr<Component>(comp));
    std::cout << id << " added " << comp->GetName() << std::endl;
  }

  void Update(float deltaTime) {
    std::cout << "
Updating GameObject: " << id << std::endl;
    for (const auto& comp : components) comp->Update(deltaTime);
  }
};

screens.title: Common Mistakes and Best Practices
screens.narratorSegment: This lesson highlights common mistakes you'll encounter and practical ways to avoid them. First, ownership errors: storing raw pointers without a clear owner often causes leaks or double deletes. Use unique_ptr for exclusive ownership and shared_ptr only when sharing ownership makes sense. Second, overusing singletons: they solve access but can lead to hidden coupling and fragile tests—keep singletons focused and small. Third, abusing inheritance for reuse creates fragile base classes where changes in a base unexpectedly break subclasses. Prefer composition when behaviors are orthogonal. Fourth, the God object anti-pattern occurs when a single class accumulates responsibilities; break responsibilities into smaller classes or components. For testing, design your code to accept dependencies via constructors or setters so you can inject mocks. Finally, always provide explicit cleanup and observe destructor messages during testing to verify resource release. These practices keep your codebase maintainable and safe as it grows. screens.title: Choosing Composition vs Inheritance
screens.narratorSegment: Deciding between composition and inheritance becomes easier when you follow a simple checklist. First, ask: do I need subtype substitutability? If you must treat objects interchangeably through a common interface in many places, inheritance with polymorphism may be the right choice. Second, ask: do behaviors change independently at runtime? If so, composition or components will let you swap behavior without changing an object's identity. Third, consider coupling and testing: if a design makes many systems depend on a base class, modifying that base risks breaking unrelated code. Fourth, examine lifetime and ownership: if components have independent lifetimes or are shared across entities, choose appropriate pointer semantics. Lastly, think about future changes: composition scales better as you add more orthogonal behaviors. A common mistake is to start with inheritance for convenience; prefer composition when you expect variability in behavior. Use this checklist during early design reviews to pick a pattern that reduces long-term maintenance cost. fullNarratorScript:
In this lesson we'll explore why composition often outperforms deep inheritance when building game objects, and how a few common design patterns help keep game code modular and maintainable. You will learn how to model 'has-a' relationships so characters, props, and systems remain flexible; we'll also examine the Singleton pattern so you can manage truly global services safely. Finally, we'll introduce the Component Pattern as the foundational approach used in modern engines to assemble game objects from small, reusable behaviors. For example, a player can contain a weapon object and swap it at runtime rather than changing its type in an inheritance tree. That simple shift improves flexibility, reduces coupling, and makes runtime behavior easier to test. Over the next screens you'll see concrete C++ code that demonstrates composing a Player with a Weapon, a robust Singleton example for managers like audio or input, and a component-based GameObject built with smart pointers. As we go, watch for common mistakes: failing to manage component lifetime, overusing singletons, or letting a class become a God object. By the end you'll be able to pick the right tool—inheritance, composition, or a pattern—for the problem at hand. Consider: when would swapping components at runtime simplify your design?

These learning objectives ground the lesson in practical skills you can apply immediately. First, you'll be able to distinguish inheritance from composition by identifying 'is-a' and 'has-a' relationships in your game designs. That distinction matters because choosing the wrong relationship can make code brittle or hard to extend. Second, you will implement composition in C++ by composing objects and delegating behavior, which lets you swap behaviors like weapons or scripts at runtime without changing core types. Third, you'll understand the Singleton pattern: how to create a single global instance for managers and when that choice introduces testing or coupling problems. Finally, you'll grasp the Component Pattern used by modern engines to assemble GameObjects from small behaviors. Each objective includes practice steps so you can verify the competency by building and running simple examples. These skills collectively reduce tight coupling, increase reuse, and make large game codebases easier to maintain and extend.

This second objectives slide maps each skill to a concrete practice you can perform. You will implement a Player that composes a Weapon object, run it, and observe how changing the weapon at runtime affects behavior. You'll write and test a Singleton for a global service such as an AudioManager, and you'll explicitly delete or disable copying to avoid accidental duplication. For the Component Pattern, you will build a Component base class and at least three concrete components—render, physics, and script—then create a GameObject that owns these components via smart pointers and calls Update on each. Verification comes from observing the printed console output for each component during an update frame and ensuring there are no memory leaks when GameObjects are destroyed. Finally, you'll evaluate when composition is a better fit than inheritance using a short design reflection: identify an entity in your game and list whether 'is-a' or 'has-a' models it best, and why.

Let's define both relationships clearly. Inheritance models an 'is-a' relationship: a derived class extends a base class and can substitute for it. Use inheritance when you need polymorphism that represents a genuine subtype — for example, an Enemy that must be treated as an Actor in a rendering or update system. Composition models a 'has-a' relationship: an object contains other objects and delegates behavior to them. In games, composition shines because behaviors like rendering, physics, or weapons are orthogonal and change at runtime. A common misconception is to use inheritance for every form of reuse: that quickly creates deep hierarchies that are rigid and lead to the fragile base class problem. Composition avoids that by keeping components focused and replaceable. A concrete example: instead of making Player inherit from SwordUser, BowUser, and MagicUser, a Player can have a Weapon object and swap instances at runtime. The practical significance is maintainability: changes in one component don't ripple across unrelated subclasses. Try this mental check: if you want to replace a behavior without changing the object's identity, prefer composition. Inheritance vs Composition means use inheritance for true subtype polymorphism and composition to enable replaceable behaviors and runtime flexibility.. In practical terms, when 'is-a' is appropriate and when to prefer 'has-a' for game entities. A concrete example makes the pattern visible, and a brief contrast helps prevent a common misconception. This matters because learners need the underlying reasoning before they can apply the idea confidently or notice where it breaks down. The main takeaway is that the concept should be understood as a meaningful pattern, not just a label on the screen.

Now we walk through a concrete C++ example that demonstrates composition clearly. The Weapon class encapsulates name and damage and exposes an Attack method. The Player contains a Weapon as a member variable and delegates attack behavior to that Weapon. This design allows changing the weapon by assignment or by swapping the underlying object, so the Player's code remains unchanged. A common nuance is how constructors initialize member objects: if you embed a Weapon object directly as a value member, you must initialize it in the Player constructor's initializer list. If you need polymorphic weapons, store pointers or smart pointers to a Weapon base and use virtual functions. Watch for ownership concerns: if you copy a Player object, value members will be copied unless you manage them explicitly. The code example in the lesson demonstrates creation, attack delegation, and ChangeWeapon. Use this pattern to keep character logic focused while letting weapons evolve independently. Composition in C++: Player and Weapon means player delegates attack to its composed weapon, enabling runtime swaps without changing player logic.. In practical terms, a concrete example showing delegation and runtime swapping. A concrete example makes the pattern visible, and a brief contrast helps prevent a common misconception. This matters because learners need the underlying reasoning before they can apply the idea confidently or notice where it breaks down. The main takeaway is that the concept should be understood as a meaningful pattern, not just a label on the screen.

The Singleton Pattern ensures a class has only one instance and provides a global point of access. It's commonly used for managers such as audio, input, or resource loading in games. The typical implementation includes a private constructor, a static member that holds the instance, a static GetInstance method to create and return the instance, and deletion of copy constructor and assignment to prevent duplicates. This pattern simplifies access to a global service, but it introduces trade-offs: singletons can increase coupling across systems, make unit testing more difficult, and create hidden dependencies. A subtle practical concern is cleanup: when the program ends you should release any allocated resources to avoid leaks. Use singletons sparingly for truly global services, and prefer dependency injection or passing references where coupling and testability matter. As a rule of thumb, ask whether the object must be globally unique; if not, prefer other techniques. Singleton Pattern in Games means use singleton for unique global services, but be mindful of coupling and testing consequences.. In practical terms, a single global instance for managers and the trade-offs involved. A concrete example makes the pattern visible, and a brief contrast helps prevent a common misconception. This matters because learners need the underlying reasoning before they can apply the idea confidently or notice where it breaks down. The main takeaway is that the concept should be understood as a meaningful pattern, not just a label on the screen.

Let's examine an AudioManager implemented as a Singleton and why you must guard against overuse. A typical AudioManager has a private constructor, static instance pointer, and a GetInstance method that lazily creates the instance. That makes it simple to call PlaySound from anywhere. The concrete benefit is convenience: systems across your codebase can request audio without passing references through layers. However, if you add unrelated responsibilities—loading resources, mixing, state tracking—the class becomes a God object, which is hard to test and change. A frequent misconception is that Singletons are inherently anti-patterns; they are a tool with trade-offs. Use them for a truly single global resource, but keep that class focused. When writing tests, provide a way to inject a mock or to reset the singleton state between tests so testing remains feasible. Finally, ensure that you provide an explicit Shutdown that deletes the instance and frees native resources to avoid leaks when your engine exits. Singleton Example and Trade-offs means singletons are convenient but can hide coupling; keep responsibilities narrow and provide cleanup and test handles.. This matters because learners need the underlying reasoning before they can apply the idea confidently or notice where it breaks down. The main takeaway is that the concept should be understood as a meaningful pattern, not just a label on the screen.

The Component Pattern treats a GameObject as a container that owns multiple small, focused components. Each component handles one responsibility: transform for position, render for drawing, physics for collision and movement, and script for game logic. This pattern enables you to add or remove behaviors at runtime by attaching or detaching components, which is particularly useful for dynamic gameplay where entities change roles or abilities. Unlike inheritance, components don't form a rigid tree; they are independent modules that the GameObject composes. Modern engines build on this idea with the Entity-Component-System architecture for performance and scale. A misconception is that components are just simple member objects; instead, design them with clear update contracts and ownership semantics. Think about lifetime: who creates a component, who destroys it, and how the GameObject's Update delegates to each component. This clarity prevents memory leaks and keeps behavior modular. The main takeaway is that the concept should be understood as a meaningful pattern, not just a label on the screen.

We'll implement a Component base class with a pure virtual Update method and three concrete components: RenderComponent, PhysicsComponent, and ScriptComponent. Each concrete class provides its own Update behavior that prints a message to the console, which helps verify the update loop. Important design details: make the destructor virtual to ensure concrete components clean up correctly; include a name or identifier for debug prints; and prefer smart pointers when adding components to a GameObject to ensure safe ownership and automatic deletion. A common pitfall is leaving Update signatures inconsistent or not marking destructors virtual, which can lead to undefined behavior when deleting derived instances through base pointers. This example uses unique_ptr ownership in the consuming GameObject to remove manual delete calls and avoid memory leaks. Implementing components this way prepares you to extend behavior without changing the GameObject interface. This lesson highlights common mistakes you'll encounter and practical ways to avoid them. First, ownership errors: storing raw pointers without a clear owner often causes leaks or double deletes. Use unique_ptr for exclusive ownership and shared_ptr only when sharing ownership makes sense. Second, overusing singletons: they solve access but can lead to hidden coupling and fragile tests—keep singletons focused and small. Third, abusing inheritance for reuse creates fragile base classes where changes in a base unexpectedly break subclasses. Prefer composition when behaviors are orthogonal. Fourth, the God object anti-pattern occurs when a single class accumulates responsibilities; break responsibilities into smaller classes or components. For testing, design your code to accept dependencies via constructors or setters so you can inject mocks. Finally, always provide explicit cleanup and observe destructor messages during testing to verify resource release. These practices keep your codebase maintainable and safe as it grows. Deciding between composition and inheritance becomes easier when you follow a simple checklist. First, ask: do I need subtype substitutability? If you must treat objects interchangeably through a common interface in many places, inheritance with polymorphism may be the right choice. Second, ask: do behaviors change independently at runtime? If so, composition or components will let you swap behavior without changing an object's identity. Third, consider coupling and testing: if a design makes many systems depend on a base class, modifying that base risks breaking unrelated code. Fourth, examine lifetime and ownership: if components have independent lifetimes or are shared across entities, choose appropriate pointer semantics. Lastly, think about future changes: composition scales better as you add more orthogonal behaviors. A common mistake is to start with inheritance for convenience; prefer composition when you expect variability in behavior. These three key concepts summarize the chapter's core lessons. Composition models 'has-a' relationships and lets you build flexible objects by combining independent behaviors. The Singleton Pattern provides a single global instance for managers like audio or input, but it introduces coupling and testing challenges if misused. The Component Pattern is a practical architecture for game objects: compose small, focused components to enable runtime changes and avoid deep inheritance hierarchies. Keep these concepts in mind when you design entities: prefer composition for replaceable behavior, use Singletons sparingly for truly unique global services, and favor components for modular, runtime-configurable objects. Here are three important pitfalls to recognize and avoid. The Component Pattern lets you compose behavior, but you must manage lifetime and ownership intentionally. The Fragile Base Class Problem appears when deep inheritance hierarchies cause unexpected breakage after base class changes; composition mitigates that risk. The God Object is an anti-pattern where a single class handles too many responsibilities, violating the Single Responsibility Principle. Recognizing these problems early will guide you to cleaner designs: break large classes into focused components, prefer composition for orthogonal features, and keep singletons lean.
